title: Compress — Budgets to Fidelity
subtitle: Per-layer budgets, prune → extract-verbatim → abstract, and the assertion that decides whether a saving was real
topics: Per-layer budgets — caps with whole-record eviction, never mid-record truncation
The compression ladder — prune (safe), extract verbatim (faithful), abstract (lossy)
Fidelity as a hard assertion — load-bearing identifiers must survive, provably
Ratio × fidelity — two axes, and only one of them shows up in the token count
The star exhibit — a 7.3x saving that the correctness stamp voids

analogy.title: Shrinking the Patient Chart
analogy.text: A specialist needs a 200-page chart briefed onto one page. First you remove what this visit doesn't need — the resolved childhood cases go (pruning). Then you copy the allergy list and current medications word for word, because 'penicillin' paraphrased as 'some antibiotics' can kill someone (extraction: load-bearing facts stay verbatim). Only the routine history gets rewritten smaller — 'three uneventful checkups 2019-2022' (abstraction). And before the brief leaves your desk, a nurse checks every allergy against the original. That final check is not bureaucracy; it is the only thing that makes the one-pager safe to act on.

antiPatterns: Abstracting identifiers — the summary that turns 'PA-1001 APPROVED, PA-1004 MANUAL_REVIEW' into 'a history of consistent approvals' saved 87% of tokens and is wrong (Q9 compressed, replay grid: FAIL — savings void)
Mid-record truncation — cutting a JSON record at the byte budget leaves the model a corrupted fact; budgets evict whole records or nothing
Fidelity by vibes — 'the summary looks fine' is not a check; only an assertion that names each surviving identifier can fail loudly enough to matter

sections.title: Budgets: the Blunt Instrument That Works
sections.body:
The budgeted assembler enforces per-layer caps — retrieval may spend so much, history so much — and when a layer overflows, it evicts whole records, oldest first, never truncating mid-JSON. That single blunt rule takes naive's ~1,695-token receipts to ~560 across all ten questions at 100% correctness (replay grid). No intelligence, no summarization — just a ceiling and a clean eviction rule.

Budgets are where compression should start, because they are the only technique with zero fidelity risk on what remains: every fact still present is still verbatim. Their ceiling is their limit — you can only evict what wasn't needed. Going below ~560 requires the ladder.

sections.title: The Ladder: Prune, Extract, Abstract
sections.body:
The compressed assembler climbs three rungs, safest first. Prune: drop what this question doesn't touch — other members' records, resolved requests (removal is lossless for what stays). Extract verbatim: the load-bearing facts survive as exact lines — PA-1004 | MANUAL_REVIEW | 65 | missing C-29881-2 — never paraphrased, because identifiers, statuses, scores and thresholds are the facts answers turn on. Abstract: only the routine remainder gets restated smaller ('2 requests total, latest 2026').

Result: ~231 median tokens, a 7.3x reduction over naive — the cheapest generative-free receipts on the board after okf. The ladder's order is the discipline: each rung is riskier than the one before, so each rung only gets what the previous rung couldn't shrink.

sections.title: The Star Exhibit: When 7.3x Is Worth Nothing
sections.body:
Open the Compare drawer on Q9 ('Summarize M-2001's history'): compressed vs naive. Compressed spends 208 tokens against naive's 1,700 — and its stamp reads ✗ FAILED. The abstraction rung swallowed PA-1004: the summary says 'consistent approvals' and the manual-review request is simply gone. The drawer prints SAVINGS VOID, and the campaign table scores compressed 90%, not 100%.

(Disclosure, per the Honesty Rule: this failure is a labeled synthetic-teaching-failure fixture — a deliberately preserved specimen of the exact failure the fidelity assertion exists to catch, the same class the kit's M18 lab produces live.) The lesson is the course's center of gravity: a token number without a correctness verdict is not a measurement. Ratio is one axis; fidelity is the other; only the pair is real.

sections.title: The Fidelity Assertion — Compression's Seatbelt
sections.code:
# The assertion that separates compression from corruption.
# (MedFlow's backend runs this same check inside the compressed assembler;
#  numbers cited: bench/results/fullgrid-compact.csv, synthetic-pre-recording.)

def compress_history(requests: list[dict], budget_tokens: int = 400) -> str:
    # 1) PRUNE: this question is about one member's history - drop the rest
    keep = [r for r in requests if r["member"] == "M-2001"]

    # 2) EXTRACT (verbatim): load-bearing line per request - NEVER paraphrased
    verbatim = [f"{r['id']} | {r['decision']} | score {r['score']}" for r in keep]

    # 3) ABSTRACT: only the routine remainder
    block = ("HISTORY (verbatim):\n  " + "\n  ".join(verbatim) +
             f"\nSUMMARY: {len(keep)} requests on file.")

    # FIDELITY CHECK: every load-bearing identifier must survive - loudly.
    for r in keep:
        assert r["id"] in block, f"LOST load-bearing id {r['id']} - refusing to ship"
    assert len(block) // 4 <= budget_tokens, "over budget - evict, don't truncate"
    return block

requests = [
    {"id": "PA-1001", "member": "M-2001", "decision": "APPROVED", "score": 100},
    {"id": "PA-1004", "member": "M-2001", "decision": "MANUAL_REVIEW", "score": 65},
    {"id": "PA-1003", "member": "M-2005", "decision": "DENIED", "score": 25},
]
print(compress_history(requests))
# Now emulate the Q9 failure: replace the verbatim rung with an LLM-style
# summary that omits PA-1004 - the assertion fires. That AssertionError is
# the difference between a compressor and a fact-shredder.

sections.question: Your compressor hits 12x reduction by abstracting everything, and spot-checks 'look fine.' WHY is this worse than the budgeted mode's boring 3x?
options: B. Abstraction without a fidelity assertion loses load-bearing facts silently; budgeted's 3x is verbatim-safe by construction, so its savings are all real — Q9 shows a 8.2x 'saving' scored as void
D. 12x exceeds the model's compression limit
sections.explanation: Ratio × fidelity: budgeted eviction can only remove, never rewrite, so what remains is exact. Unchecked abstraction produced Q9's dropped PA-1004 — 208 tokens, FAIL, savings void (replay grid). A smaller number that might be wrong loses to a bigger number that is certainly right.

sections.question: WHEN is the abstract rung of the ladder the correct tool?
options: A. Whenever the budget is tight
B. For the routine remainder only — content where no downstream decision turns on exact wording — and always behind an assertion that the load-bearing facts survived the whole block
C. For identifiers, since they compress well
D. Never — extraction should always suffice
sections.explanation: The ladder's order is safest-first: prune what's irrelevant, extract the decision-bearing facts verbatim, and only then abstract the narrative filler. The kit's M18 rule is blunt: never abstract an exact identifier or a load-bearing decision — and the assertion is what makes the rule enforceable rather than aspirational.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong
items: Celebrating the ratio — dashboards report 'tokens saved' with no correctness column; Q9's 8.2x void saving sails through review until a clinician asks where PA-1004 went
Budget by truncation — cutting at exactly N tokens mid-record corrupts the last fact; the model then reasons confidently from half a JSON object
Assertion theater — a fidelity check that only samples, or only warns, converts the seatbelt back into decoration; it must enumerate every load-bearing id and it must throw

takeaway: Compression is a safest-first ladder — prune, extract verbatim, then abstract — and a saving only exists if the fidelity assertion proves the load-bearing facts survived.
labUnderstand: Read Q5 receipts down the ladder (naive 1,704 → budgeted 569 → compressed 247), then open the Compare drawer on Q9 and meet the 208-token receipt whose stamp voids it. You chart exactly which rung dropped PA-1004.
labBuild: With Claude writing the code, build compress_audit.py: run the ladder over M-2001's history, assert identifier survival, and report ratio AND fidelity per rung. Break it on purpose by swapping the extract rung for abstraction and watch your own assertion fire — proving it's protection, not decoration.
